customLessons.title: Systems in Animals and Plants
objectives: Identify and describe the functions of major body systems in animals: skeletal, muscular, digestive, respiratory, and circulatory systems.
Describe the two major plant systems: root system (anchoring, absorption) and shoot system (stem, leaves, flowers, fruits for photosynthesis, reproduction, and support).
Perform a hands-on diagram labeling and explanation performance task illustrating how plant and animal systems maintain life.
customLessons.content:
GRADE 4 SCIENCE — LESSON 1: Systems in Animals and Plants
(Validated DepEd MATATAG Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
Describe the functions of major organs and organ systems in animals and plants.

ORGAN SYSTEMS IN ANIMALS:
• Skeletal System: Internal framework of bones that supports and protects vital organs (e.g., skull protects brain, ribs protect heart and lungs).
• Muscular System: Muscle tissues that work together with bones to create body movement (running, jumping, posture).
• Digestive System: Breaks down and processes food so the body can absorb essential nutrients and energy.
• Respiratory System: Takes in life-sustaining oxygen gas from the air and removes carbon dioxide waste from the body.
• Circulatory System: Heart and blood vessels that pump and transport oxygen, nutrients, and fluids throughout the body.

MAJOR SYSTEMS IN PLANTS:
Plants have two interconnected organ systems:
1. Root System: Underground roots that anchor the plant securely in the soil and absorb water and dissolved mineral nutrients.
2. Shoot System: Aerial parts including the stem, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
   - Leaves: Carry out photosynthesis to manufacture food.
   - Stem: Provides physical support and transports water and sap.
   - Flowers & Fruits: Carry out reproduction and seed development.

INTERACTIVE ACTIVITY: Which System?
• Situation 1: A boy runs across the school playground → Skeletal and Muscular Systems collaborate.
• Situation 2: A girl inhales fresh morning air → Respiratory System.
• Situation 3: A plant absorbs rainwater after a thunderstorm → Root System.
• Situation 4: An athlete digests an energy snack → Digestive and Circulatory Systems.

PERFORMANCE TASK: Diagram Investigation
Learners observe an illustrated diagram of a flowering plant and human torso, label the primary root/shoot and organ systems, and write a 2-sentence explanation of each system's essential function.

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Animal systems (skeletal, muscular, digestive, respiratory, circulatory) coordinate to maintain life.
• Plants rely on two systems: Root System (underground anchor/intake) and Shoot System (aerial food production and reproduction).
• Organs work together in teams called organ systems.

customLessons.content:
GRADE 4 SCIENCE — LESSON 2: Plant and Animal Habitats
(Validated DepEd MATATAG Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
Identify and describe plant and animal habitats and explain how organisms depend on their habitat for survival.

WHAT IS A HABITAT?
A habitat is the natural place where an organism lives, grows, and gets what it needs to survive.

FOUR BASIC NEEDS PROVIDED BY HABITATS:
1. Food: Nutrients needed for energy and growth.
2. Water: Essential for hydration and cellular function.
3. Shelter: Protection from predators, harsh heat, and bad weather.
4. Space: Adequate area to move, hunt, grow roots, and raise offspring.

MAJOR HABITAT TYPES:
• Terrestrial Habitats (Land): Tropical rainforests, open grasslands, farms, and mountains. (Examples: Carabao, narra tree, Philippine deer).
• Aquatic Habitats (Water): Freshwater (rivers, lakes, ponds like Laguna de Bay) and Marine (coral reefs, open ocean). (Examples: Tilapia, bangus, water lilies, sea turtles).
• Scientific Note on 'Aerial Habitats': Some animals spend much of their time moving or feeding in the air (eagles, fruit bats, dragonflies, butterflies). However, they rest, nest, and reproduce on land, trees, cliffs, or water. Therefore, 'aerial' is accurately described as an environment used primarily for movement and feeding rather than a permanent home.

INTERACTIVE ACTIVITY: Match the Organism to its Habitat!
• Bangus (Milkfish) → Aquatic freshwater/marine habitat
• Carabao → Terrestrial agricultural grassland
• Philippine Eagle → High canopy trees and forest airspace
• Water Lily → Aquatic pond surface

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Habitats provide food, water, shelter, and space.
• Land habitats are terrestrial; water habitats are aquatic.
• Aerial environments are used for movement and foraging, with organisms resting on land/trees.
• Protecting natural habitats is crucial for species preservation.

customLessons.title: Life Cycles of Plants and Animals
objectives: Define a life cycle and describe the developmental stages of flowering plants and common animals.
Sequence the life cycle stages of flowering plants (Seed → Germination → Seedling → Mature Plant → Flower/Fruit → Seeds).
Compare developmental stages in butterflies (Egg → Caterpillar → Pupa → Adult) and chickens (Egg → Chick → Adult).
customLessons.content:
GRADE 4 SCIENCE — LESSON 3: Life Cycles of Plants and Animals
(Validated DepEd MATATAG Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
Describe and compare the stages in the life cycle of plants and animals.

WHAT IS A LIFE CYCLE?
A life cycle refers to the series of developmental stages an organism goes through as it grows, develops, and reproduces, ensuring the continuation of its species.

FLOWERING PLANT LIFE CYCLE:
Many flowering plants begin their life cycle from a seed. (Scientific note: Clarified that this applies specifically to flowering plants, as other plants reproduce via spores or vegetative parts).
• Stage 1: Seed (Dormant seed containing embryo and stored food)
• Stage 2: Germination (Sprouting root and shoot emerge with water and warmth)
• Stage 3: Seedling (Young delicate plant with first green leaves)
• Stage 4: Mature Plant (Full-sized plant with sturdy stem and foliage)
• Stage 5: Flower/Fruit (Flowers bloom, pollination occurs, and fruit forms)
• Stage 6: New Seeds (Dispersed to begin the next generation)
Flowchart: Seed → Germination → Seedling → Mature Plant → Flower/Fruit → Seeds

ANIMAL LIFE CYCLES:
• Butterfly (Complete Metamorphosis):
  Egg → Larva (Caterpillar) → Pupa (Chrysalis) → Adult Butterfly
• Chicken:
  Egg → Chick → Young Chicken → Adult Chicken

INTERACTIVE ACTIVITY: Whose Life Cycle Is It?
1. Egg → Larva → Pupa → Adult → Butterfly
2. Seed → Germination → Seedling → Mature Plant → Flower/Fruit → Flowering Plant (e.g. Tomato / Mongo)
3. Egg → Chick → Adult Chicken → Chicken

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• A life cycle shows the continuous stages of growth and reproduction.
• Flowering plant cycle: Seed → Germination → Seedling → Mature Plant → Flower/Fruit → Seeds.
• Butterfly transforms through complete metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult).
• Life cycles ensure living things produce new generations.

customLessons.content:
GRADE 4 SCIENCE — LESSON 4: Animals and the Food They Eat
(Validated DepEd MATATAG Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
Classify animals according to what they eat (herbivores, carnivores, and omnivores).

THREE DIETARY CLASSIFICATIONS:
• Herbivores — Animals that mainly eat plants (grass, leaves, fruits, stems, seeds).
  - Philippine Examples: Carabao, goat, cow, deer, rabbit, caterpillar.
  - Feeding Adaptations: Broad, flat molars to grind tough plant fibers.
• Carnivores — Animals that mainly eat other animals (meat, fish, insects).
  - Philippine Examples: Philippine Eagle, cobra/snake, crocodile, shark, lion, tiger.
  - Feeding Adaptations: Sharp pointed canine teeth, hooked beaks, and sharp talons to catch and tear flesh.
• Omnivores — Animals that eat both plants and animals.
  - Philippine Examples: Chicken (eats grains and insects), pig (eats vegetable slops and small fish), duck, bear, and humans.
  - Feeding Adaptations: Versatile combination of sharp front incisors/canines and flat grinding molars.

SCIENTIFIC MEMORY AID:
• Herbivores → Mainly eat plants
• Carnivores → Mainly eat other animals
• Omnivores → Eat both plants and animals

INTERACTIVE ACTIVITY: Sort by Diet!
• Cow → Grass → Herbivore
• Goat → Leaves and shrubs → Herbivore
• Philippine Eagle → Monkeys, snakes, fish → Carnivore
• Snake → Frogs and mice → Carnivore
• Chicken → Rice grains and worms → Omnivore
• Pig → Roots, vegetables, and leftover meat → Omnivore

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Animals are grouped by their diet: herbivores (plant eaters), carnivores (meat eaters), and omnivores (both).
• A chicken is an omnivore because it pecks at grains and catches small insects.
• Teeth structure matches an animal's diet.

objectives: Construct and interpret simple food chains in Philippine ecosystems.

customLessons.content:
GRADE 4 SCIENCE — LESSON 5: Food Chains
(Validated DepEd MATATAG Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
Construct simple food chains in Philippine habitats and explain energy flow between organisms.

WHAT IS A FOOD CHAIN?
A food chain shows the linear sequence of who eats whom in an ecosystem, showing how food energy passes from one living thing to another.

ROLES IN A FOOD CHAIN:
• Producer: Green plants that capture sunlight to manufacture their own food through photosynthesis (e.g., grass, rice plant, algae).
• Primary Consumer: Herbivores that feed directly on producers (e.g., grasshopper, caterpillar).
• Secondary Consumer: Carnivores or omnivores that feed on primary consumers (e.g., frog, chicken).
• Tertiary Consumer / Other Consumers: Predators that feed on secondary consumers (e.g., snake, hawk).
• Decomposers: Fungi and soil bacteria that recycle nutrients back into soil.

CRUCIAL RULE ON FOOD CHAIN ARROWS:
The arrow points in the direction of energy flow: from the organism being eaten TO the organism that eats it!
Example: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake
• Grass is eaten by Grasshopper (arrow points to Grasshopper)
• Grasshopper is eaten by Frog (arrow points to Frog)
• Frog is eaten by Snake (arrow points to Snake)

PHILIPPINE RICE FIELD FOOD CHAIN:
Rice Plant (Producer) → Grasshopper (Primary Consumer) → Field Frog (Secondary Consumer) → Snake (Tertiary Consumer)

INTERACTIVE ACTIVITY: Build the Food Chain!
Arrange in the correct energy sequence:
• Organisms: Frog, Grass, Snake, Grasshopper
• Correct Order: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• All food chains begin with a producer (green plant) fueled by sunlight.
• Arrows always point to the consumer that eats the organism.
• A disruption in one link (e.g. pesticide wiping out frogs) causes grasshopper populations to surge.

customLessons.content:
GRADE 4 SCIENCE — LESSON 6: Water and Living Things
(Validated DepEd MATATAG Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
Explain the importance of water to plants and animals and identify freshwater sources.

FRESHWATER SOURCES:
Living things depend on freshwater from:
• Rainwater (precipitation replenishment)
• Rivers, streams, and creeks
• Freshwater lakes (e.g., Laguna de Bay, Lake Taal)
• Groundwater (springs, deep wells, and aquifers)

IMPORTANCE OF WATER TO PLANTS:
• Essential Material for Photosynthesis: Green plants use water as one of the essential raw materials (combined with sunlight and carbon dioxide) to manufacture food (glucose).
• Absorption by Roots: Roots are the primary organs that absorb moisture and dissolved soil minerals, transporting them upward through the stem.
• Structural Support: Water fills plant cells, creating turgor pressure that keeps stems and leaves upright and crisp. Without water, plants wilt.

IMPORTANCE OF WATER TO ANIMALS AND HUMANS:
• Animals drink water directly or obtain moisture indirectly through their food and moist environments (e.g., frogs absorb moisture through their skin and surroundings).
• Water helps transport nutrients and oxygen in blood plasma.
• Water regulates body temperature and helps flush out metabolic body wastes.

INTERACTIVE ACTIVITY: Water in Nature!
1. Why do wilted leaves stand tall after watering? → Water enters roots and restores internal cell firmness.
2. How does a dog cool down on a hot summer afternoon? → Panting releases moisture, cooling the body.
3. What freshwater source supplies water to community irrigation? → Rivers, dams, and lakes.

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Rain, rivers, lakes, and groundwater supply freshwater to living organisms.
• Plants absorb water through roots as a necessary raw material for photosynthesis.
• Animals need water to digest food, circulate nutrients, and stay cool.

customLessons.title: Soil and Plant Growth
objectives: Identify components of healthy soil: rock fragments, organic matter, air, water, and living organisms.
Compare the characteristics and particle sizes of Sandy, Clay, Silt, and Loam soils.
Conduct a simple guided investigation to determine how different soil types affect drainage and plant growth.
customLessons.content:
GRADE 4 SCIENCE — LESSON 7: Soil and Plant Growth
(Validated DepEd MATATAG Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
Investigate the characteristics of different types of soil and how they affect plant growth.

COMPONENTS OF SOIL:
Soil is made up of:
• Rock fragments: Tiny particles broken down from large rocks over time.
• Organic matter: Decayed fallen leaves, dead plants, and decomposing animal matter (humus).
• Air: Pockets of oxygen needed by root cells to respire.
• Water: Dissolves soil nutrients for plant absorption.
• Living organisms: Earthworms, beneficial bacteria, and fungi that aerate soil.

FOUR MAIN SOIL TYPES & PARTICLE SIZES:
1. Sandy Soil: Large, coarse particles. Rough texture, drains water very quickly, low water-holding capacity.
2. Clay Soil: Very fine, microscopic particles. Smooth and sticky when wet, hard when dry. Slow drainage, high water-holding capacity.
3. Silt Soil: Fine particles that are smaller than sand but larger than clay. Smooth, flour-like texture, moderate water retention.
4. Loam Soil: Balanced mixture of sand, silt, clay, and rich organic matter. It holds enough moisture while allowing proper drainage and root aeration, making it the most suitable soil for growing garden plants!

HOW SOIL SUPPORTS PLANT GROWTH:
Soil anchors roots firmly, provides access to dissolved mineral nutrients (Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium), and supplies essential root air pockets.

GUIDED INVESTIGATION: Soil Drainage & Water Holding
• Materials: 3 identical clear plastic cups with small drainage holes, labeled: Sand, Clay, Loam. Measuring cup, 100 mL water per cup, stopwatch.
• Procedure:
  1. Fill each cup halfway with its designated soil type.
  2. Pour 100 mL of water simultaneously into each cup.
  3. Measure the volume of water drained after 3 minutes.
• Observations:
  - Sand cup: Drains water rapidly; low water retained.
  - Clay cup: Water ponds on surface; very slow trickle.
  - Loam cup: Drains steady excess water while soil stays moist and dark.
• Conclusion: Different soil types possess different water-holding and drainage properties. Loam provides the ideal balance for root growth.

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Fertile soil contains minerals, organic matter, air, water, and organisms.
• Silt particles are smaller than sand but larger than clay.
• Loam is a balanced mixture ideal for crops and vegetables.
• Proper soil allows both root breathing and adequate moisture retention.

• Soil water: Dissolves minerals for root uptake

• Silt: Smaller than sand but larger than clay; smooth silky feel
• Clay: Microscopic particles, sticky when wet, slow drainage
• Loam: Balanced mix of sand, silt, clay, and rich humus — the champion for plants!

questions.text: Which body system provides an internal framework to support and protect vital organs? | A: Respiratory System B: Skeletal System C: Digestive System D: Circulatory System
Which body system works together with bones to enable walking, running, and jumping? | A: Muscular System B: Circulatory System C: Root System D: Shoot System
Which organ system processes the food we eat and helps the body absorb vital nutrients? | A: Respiratory System B: Skeletal System C: Digestive System D: Circulatory System
Which plant system anchors the plant securely in the soil and absorbs water and dissolved minerals? | A: Shoot System B: Root System C: Skeletal System D: Muscular System
Which plant system includes the stem, leaves, flowers, and fruits responsible for photosynthesis and reproduction? | A: Root System B: Shoot System C: Digestive System D: Circulatory System
What is the natural place where an organism lives and obtains food, water, shelter, and space? | A: Ecosystem web B: Habitat C: Weather D: Metamorphosis
Which of the following is an example of an aquatic habitat in the Philippines? | A: Sierra Madre forest B: Baguio pine ridge C: Laguna de Bay freshwater lake D: Rice paddy dike

What four basic survival needs does a natural habitat provide to plants and animals? | A: Food, water, shelter, and space B: Sunlight, gold, wind, and iron C: Rocks, noise, clothes, and tools D: Electricity, glass, salt, and roads

Why is the air described as an environment used mainly for movement and feeding rather than a permanent aerial habitat? | A: Flying animals cannot breathe air B: Flying animals like eagles and bats must land on trees or cliffs to rest, nest, and reproduce C: Birds never touch the ground D: Insects live permanently in clouds

What happens to forest wildlife when trees are cut down and their habitat is destroyed? | A: They lose their food, shelter, and space, threatening their survival B: They instantly double in population C: They turn into aquatic animals D: They grow bigger wings

questions.topic: Life Cycles of Plants and Animals
questions.text: What is a life cycle in living organisms? | A: A bicycle for animals B: The stages an organism goes through as it grows and develops C: The food an animal eats D: How fast an organism runs

questions.topic: Life Cycles of Plants and Animals
questions.text: For many flowering plants, from what structure does their life cycle begin? | A: Seed B: Fruit C: Leaf D: Flower petal

questions.topic: Life Cycles of Plants and Animals
questions.text: What is the resting, transforming stage in a butterfly's life cycle before it emerges as an adult? | A: Caterpillar B: Pupa (Chrysalis) C: Chick D: Sprout

questions.topic: Life Cycles of Plants and Animals
questions.text: Which sequence correctly represents the developmental stages of a chicken? | A: Chick → Egg → Adult Chicken B: Egg → Chick → Adult Chicken C: Adult Chicken → Chick → Egg D: Egg → Pupa → Chick

questions.topic: Life Cycles of Plants and Animals
questions.text: Why do scientists use flowcharts or circular diagrams when illustrating life cycles? | A: To show the order of stages clearly and demonstrate how life continues across generations B: Because circles are easy to draw C: To prove animals do not grow D: To hide the developmental stages

questions.topic: Animals and the Food They Eat
questions.text: What do herbivorous animals like carabaos, cows, and goats mainly eat? | A: Plants such as grass, leaves, and fruits B: Meat and fish only C: Insects and spiders D: Bones and shells

questions.topic: Animals and the Food They Eat
questions.text: Which of the following Philippine animals is a carnivore that feeds on other animals? | A: Carabao B: Goat C: Philippine Eagle D: Grasshopper

questions.topic: Animals and the Food They Eat
questions.text: Why is a chicken classified as an omnivore? | A: It eats both plant seeds/grains and small insects/worms B: It eats only tall trees C: It hunts ocean sharks D: It drinks only nectar

questions.topic: Animals and the Food They Eat
questions.text: An animal with broad, flat molars adapted for grinding tough fibrous grass belongs to which group? | A: Carnivore B: Herbivore C: Scavenger D: Parasite

questions.topic: Animals and the Food They Eat
questions.text: How do omnivorous animals survive in diverse environments? | A: They do not need any food B: They eat only rocks C: They can obtain energy from both plant materials and animal foods D: They only eat at night

What does a simple food chain represent in an ecosystem? | A: A list of all animals in a zoo B: The feeding relationships and pathway of food energy from one organism to another C: How plants absorb water from soil D: The physical size of different animals
In the food chain: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake, which organism is the producer? | A: Snake B: Frog C: Grass D: Grasshopper
In the food chain: Rice Plant → Locust → Field Frog → Cobra, which organism acts as a tertiary consumer? | A: Rice Plant B: Locust C: Field Frog D: Cobra

What is the meaning of an arrow pointing from grass to grasshopper in a food chain diagram? | A: The grass eats the grasshopper B: Energy flows from the grass to the grasshopper that eats it C: The grasshopper protects the grass D: Grasshoppers turn into grass

If all frogs in a garden pond ecosystem disappear, what is the most likely immediate effect on the food chain? | A: The grasshopper population will increase because frogs are no longer eating them B: Snakes will multiply rapidly C: Grass will disappear instantly D: Water will stop flowing
What main plant part is responsible for absorbing water and dissolved minerals from the soil? | A: Roots B: Petals C: Bark D: Seeds

Which of the following is a vital freshwater source that provides drinking water for humans, animals, and agricultural crops? | A: Ocean saltwater B: Rivers, lakes, and groundwater C: Bleach D: Muddy puddle

Why is water essential for green plants during photosynthesis? | A: Water cools the ground B: Water turns leaves brown C: Plants use water as one of the raw materials combined with light and carbon dioxide to produce food D: Water replaces sunlight

How does a tree survive during sunny days when water in the soil is scarce? | A: Deep root systems absorb groundwater and leaves regulate water loss B: It walks to a river C: It stops needing sunlight D: It turns into stone

Why do living animals need to drink water or obtain moisture from their food? | A: To stay asleep B: Water is only used for swimming C: To transport nutrients in the body, regulate temperature, and maintain healthy cell function D: To prevent breathing
Which of the following is an essential component of healthy, fertile soil? | A: Pure plastic B: Glass fragments C: Aluminum foil D: Rock fragments, organic matter, air, water, and living organisms
Which soil type has large particles, feels rough to the touch, and drains water very quickly? | A: Clay soil B: Sandy soil C: Loam soil D: Mud

How does the particle size of silt compare with sand and clay? | A: Silt particles are smaller than sand but larger than clay B: Silt particles are larger than pebbles C: Silt particles are the biggest in nature D: Silt has no particles

Why is loam soil considered the most suitable soil type for growing most garden vegetables and crops? | A: It contains only stones B: It repels all moisture C: It has a balanced mixture of sand, silt, and clay with rich organic matter that retains moisture while allowing drainage D: It is made of pure chalk

In a simple soil investigation comparing sand, clay, and loam, what can pupils conclude after pouring equal amounts of water through each soil cup? | A: Different soil types have different water-holding and drainage capacities affecting plant growth B: All soils drain water at the exact same second C: Water disappears completely inside sand D: Plants do not need soil
